extracted.intended_audience: NIH/CSR staff, scientific review officers, peer reviewers, study section chairs, and researchers who participate in or study NIH peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, evaluation criteria, and metrics CSR uses to assess the quality, integrity, and operations of NIH peer review (meeting formats, panel composition, scoring behavior, anonymization, and programmatic interventions such as ECR and ENQUIRE). Targeted at improving fairness, recruitment, and identification of high-impact science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission: fair, independent, expert, and timely reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: To see that NIH grant applications receive fair, independent, expert, and timely scientific reviews – free from inappropriate influences – so that NIH can fund the most promising research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mission statement functions as an overarching evaluative standard: reviews should be fair (impartial), independent (no inappropriate influence), expert (reviewers with appropriate expertise), and timely. Operational measures and programs are assessed against these goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality is critical for candor
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidentiality is critical for candor in discussion and evaluation, and thus impacts the very basis of the peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain confidentiality in pre-meeting training and opening meeting statements; confidentiality is treated as essential to enable frank reviewer discussion and to preserve integrity of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity: follow-up on every allegation
rubrics_metrics.description: We follow up on every allegation. Cases are referred to the Office of Management Assessment (OMA) – independent of CSR - an investigative unit conducts fact-finding, investigations, and issues a report of findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible actions include withdrawal of application, removal of reviewers from peer review committees, notification of investigator/reviewer’s institution (which may lead to personnel actions), pursuing suspension and debarment, and referral to other agencies for criminal violations. Integrity adjudication is formal and documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting channels and ease of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Making Reporting Easier: For concerns or questions about possible violations of peer review integrity, please contact your Scientific Review Officer, or the CSR Review Integrity Officer at csrrio@mail.nih.gov, or the NIH Review Policy Officer at peerreview@nih.gov.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CSR emphasizes multiple reporting avenues (SRO, CSR Review Integrity Officer, NIH Review Policy Officer) and regular discussion of integrity and reporting during reviewer training and meeting openings to encourage reporting of concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching referral of applications to reviewer expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical to success – matching referral of applications and reviewer expertise to redefined scientific scope of study sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When redefining study section scope (e.g., via ENQUIRE), a primary evaluative criterion is whether application referral mechanisms and reviewer rosters align with the scientific scope so the highest-impact science is identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: ENQUIRE: systematic, data-driven, continuous panel evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: CSR ENQUIRE integrates data and input from multiple stakeholders to determine whether changes in study section focus or scope are needed, with special consideration of emerging science. It is a systematic, data-driven, continuous process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process features: clusters of study sections formed by scientific topic, stakeholder input (external scientific community, NIH programs, CSR staff), iterative refinement based on experience. Approximately 20% of CSR study sections evaluated each year so each is evaluated every 5 years. Evaluation leads to concrete structural actions (see next metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: ENQUIRE: possible actions following evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple Possible Actions Follow: Change in scientific guidelines; Merge study sections; Create new study sections; Redistribute areas across study sections; Add emerging areas of science; Eliminate study sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ENQUIRE evaluations are explicitly tied to operational changes in study-section organization and scope; these are the set of remedies CSR may pursue when ENQUIRE identifies mismatches or opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymization (redaction) effectiveness and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: CSR Anonymization Study: 1,200 previously reviewed applications, both full and redacted, were used. Findings: Redaction does not affect the scores for grants submitted by African-American investigators; redaction slightly worsens the scores for grants submitted by White investigators (small but statistically significant); redaction was not very effective at preventing identification of the investigator (>20% of reviewers correctly identified the investigator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative dimensions include effect of redaction on scores for demographic groups and the success rate of de-identification (identifiability). The study assesses both bias mitigation and practical limits of anonymization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commensuration bias (use of criteria scores to derive overall impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commensuration Bias Study: Do reviewers use criteria scores to derive overall impact scores differently for Black versus White applicants? Outcome: Small but statistically significant commensuration bias, but these effects are very small and do not account for the much larger disparities in overall impact scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metric: consistency in translating criterion-level scores into overall impact scores across applicant demographic groups. Analyses assess whether differential weighting or mapping contributes to score disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking consistency across study sections (Intra-IRG Ranking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intra-IRG Ranking Study: Will reviewer rankings of the top 20% of applications across study sections within an integrated review group (IRG) reveal differences in the quality of science among the study sections? Outcome: No large differences in quality evident; rankings were related to reviewers’ familiarity with the science and adjusting for reviewer familiarity further reduced ranking differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criteria include between-section rank-order consistency and the influence of reviewer familiarity; analyses should control for reviewer familiarity to assess true differences in application quality across sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring granularity and score compression (Half-Point Pilot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Half Point Pilot: Will allowing reviewers to use 0.5 increments for scoring (e.g., 1.5, 2.0, 2.5) improve score compression? Outcome: Half-point option did not significantly improve score compression for most study sections or significantly alter rank order of applications. CSR will not implement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: whether increasing score granularity reduces score clustering and changes rank order. Decision based on statistical effects on compression and rank stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting format effects (in-person vs virtual vs hybrid)
rubrics_metrics.description: How Does Meeting Format Affect Review? Surveys (~8,000 reviewers in 2020 and 2021) and analyses compared in-person, virtual, and hybrid meetings on reviewer preference, perceived meeting quality, engagement (attention span), meeting duration, reviewer recruitment/roster composition, and scoring behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key findings used as evaluation criteria: preference distribution (≈40% prefer in-person, ~1/3 prefer virtual, ~1/3 no preference), similar quality ratings for in-person and virtual, no significant change in score distributions, but engagement suffered in virtual meetings (46% reported shorter attention span) and virtual meetings tended to be longer. Also analyze differences by gender and career stage in format preference and any effects on recruitment and representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtual platform specific metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: How Does Use of a Virtual Platform Affect Review Meetings? CSR held >600 virtual review meetings (Mar–Aug 2020) and surveyed reviewers, SROs, and staff; quantitative analyses of meeting duration and roster composition (n=143 matched meetings) were performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation uses operational metrics: number of virtual meetings, stakeholder survey responses (reviewers, scientific review officers, staff), matched quantitative analyses of meeting duration and roster composition, and measures of whether virtual format changed female/minority representation, career-stage distribution, or proportion of new reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer engagement as an evaluative dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagement appeared to suffer in virtual meetings: nearly half of all reviewers (46%) reported having a shorter attention span during a virtual meeting and quantitative analyses suggest virtual meetings tend to be longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engagement is measured via self-reported attention span, meeting duration, and qualitative comments; CSR indicates engagement will be a focal point for continuing evaluation of virtual platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Career Reviewer (ECR) program goals and evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The ECR Program enriches the pool of NIH reviewers and gives scientists peer review experience applicable to crafting competitive applications. To date 10,109 individuals trained; 1,306 former ECRs have served as members of standing study sections or are currently members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planned analyses to evaluate program effectiveness include: comparing success rates for R01s submitted by ECRs versus early career researchers (matched for career characteristics), assessing geographic distribution and institution type of ECRs and those recruited to review, and surveying ECRs to identify areas for program improvement. Metrics capture recruitment pipeline, retention to study sections, and downstream grant success.
